title: [Rear View] ASEAN postscript: Marcos forgot who his real audience is
summary: Marcos and Trump took center stage as two men in the early stages of lameduckery. Both carry deep trust deficits, and both have suffered major political reversals.

blocks.text: To be fair, chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and hosting its summit is an obligation. But the Marcos administration couldn’t resist turning it into a vanity project.

Parts of Metro Manila plagued by squalor amid plenty were transformed, for three days, into a painted-over, water-hosed showcase of the true, the good, and the beautiful. Protest groups were asked to keep the summit a protest-free zone, as though airing grievances while guests were in town were a breach of manners.

When the protesters marched anyway, police met them with truncheons and shields. More than 300 were arrested across Metro Manila and nearby provinces, loaded into police vans and held at Camp Bagong Diwa until Air Force One had cleared the tarmac. The administration conveniently forgot that constitutional rights are not suspended when foreign guests arrive.
With his term nearing its close, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is eager to claim his spot on the global stage.

He has spoken all year of the region’s “defining moment,” but has had little to say about his own administration’s, confronted as it is by rising inflation, gas prices, unmitigated corruption, and the creeping breakdown of public services.

He wanted to make a good impression on the visiting heads of state, his regional peers, and the leaders of the major powers, above all US President Donald Trump. He forgot that such impressions are fleeting; these leaders have their own troubles at home. The lasting impression lies with the people, who saw in the hosting another example of an administration out of touch with daily realities.

Marcos grinned throughout his face-to-face meetings with Trump, even arranging a brief reunion between Trump and his mother, the former first lady, wheelchair-bound but still able to turn on the charm for a man she first met decades ago on the New York party circuit.
Posting on Truth Social as he left Manila, Trump praised Marcos as “a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance.” It was the money shot Marcos had longed for.

blocks.text: Marcos and Trump took center stage as two men in the early stages of lameduckery. Both carry deep trust deficits, and both have suffered major political reversals. In the wake of his party’s resounding midterm defeat, Trump, true to form, has doubled down on his unpopular agenda. Faced with mounting economic woes, Marcos would rather focus on his political survival.

The global stage offers refuge and respite, however brief, a place where he can shine and be applauded by his peers. After the handshakes, the gala dinners, the gabfest, and the photo opportunities, the delegations flew home, perhaps impressed by the hospitality. But foreign leaders and their entourages will not vote in 2028.

The President wanted the world to watch him. For three days, Metro Manila became a stage set and a conflict zone. We got an extended holiday, but commuters were stranded by road closures, vendors were cleared from motorcade routes, and protesters were loaded into police vans for exercising a constitutional right their President swore to defend.
In trying to impress the world, the President forgot who his real audience is, and they were never inside the convention hall. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.
